name: Chile
summary: Children, parents and a spouse are forced heirs: half the estate is reserved to them (Civil Code art. 1182), and a further quarter (the cuarta de mejoras) can go only to certain family members. Only about a quarter is free to give by will. Chilean heirs can also claim a share of Chilean assets when a foreign law would deny it. Chile has no trust law and allows only non-profit foundations.
reserved_share: Half the estate is the legítima rigorosa, shared by children (or, lacking children, ascendants and spouse) (Código Civil arts. 1182, 1183); a quarter is the cuarta de mejoras, left only to descendants, ascendants or spouse (art. 1184); a quarter is free to dispose of. Spouse's and ascendants' shares depend on who concurs.
foreign_law_note: Succession is governed by the law of the deceased's last domicile (Código Civil art. 955). Chilean heirs have a right to take their Chilean-law share from Chilean assets when a foreign succession law gives them less (arts. 15, 16 and 998; the 'derecho de prelación'). No general choice of the law of nationality was found.
trust_note: There is no trust law; the nearest devices are the fideicomiso (propiedad fiduciaria, Civil Code arts. 732 ff.) and the fiducia in the Ley de Bancos, both narrow. Chile is not a party to the Hague Trusts Convention. Foundations (Civil Code arts. 545 ff., Ley 20.500) must be non-profit and serve a defined purpose; a private family foundation was not found.
open_questions: The text of arts. 1184 and 998 as currently in force was read only through secondary sources; confirm at bcn.cl.
A 2020 law-journal article argues for repealing the cuarta de mejoras; no repeal was found, and bills may be pending.
Treatment of foreign trusts by Chile's courts and the SII was not sourced.
